The selfish-gene reading of The Secret Agent makes it less romantic and far more precise. Adolf Verloc and his work as a spy for an unnamed country (presumably Russia). The Secret Agent is one of Conrad's later political novels in which he moved away from his tales of seafaring.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. It also deals with exploitation of the vulnerable in Verloc's relationship with his brother-in-law Stevie, who has an intellectual disability. Conrad's gloomy portrait of London depicted in the novel was influenced by Charles Dickens' Bleak House.

The feeling that The Secret Agent means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. The novel was adapted as a stage play by Conrad and has since been adapted for film, TV, radio and opera. Because of its terrorism theme, it was one of the three works of literature most cited in the American media two weeks after the September 11 attacks.

Nothing in The Secret Agent was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Set in Soho, London in 1886, the novel follows the life of Adolf Verloc, a secret agent. Verloc is also a businessman who owns a shop which sells pornographic material, contraceptives and bric-a-brac.

The psychology underneath The Secret Agent is simpler and older than the story on top. Stevie has a mental disability (possibly autism) which causes him to be excitable; his sister, Verloc's wife, attends to him, treating him more as a son than as a brother. Verloc's friends are a group of anarchists of which Comrade Ossipon, Michaelis and "The Professor" are the most prominent.

Behind The Secret Agent sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. Although largely ineffectual as terrorists, their actions are known to the police. The group produces anarchist literature in the form of pamphlets entitled F.P., an acronym for The Future of the Proletariat.

The nihilist does not deny The Secret Agent — he only refuses to flatter it. The novel begins in Verloc's home, as he and his wife discuss the trivialities of everyday life, which introduces the reader to Verloc's family. Soon after, Verloc leaves to meet Mr Vladimir, the new First Secretary in the embassy of a foreign country, for whom he works as an agent provocateur.

What culture calls destiny in The Secret Agent is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Vladimir informs Verloc that from reviewing his service history he is far from an exemplary model of a secret agent and to redeem himself, must carry out an operation – the destruction of Greenwich Observatory by a bomb. Vladimir explains that Britain's lax attitude to anarchism endangers his country and he thinks that an attack on 'science', in vogue amongst the public, will provide the necessary outrage for suppression.

The genes do not care about The Secret Agent; they care about copies. Verloc later meets his friends, who discuss politics and law, and the notion of a communist revolution. Unbeknownst to the group, Stevie, Verloc's brother-in-law, overhears the conversation, which greatly disturbs him.

Take away the meaning and The Secret Agent still functions — that is the disturbing part. Comrade Ossipon meets The Professor, who discusses having given explosives to Verloc. The Professor describes the nature of the bomb he carries in his coat at all times: it allows him to press a button which will kill him and those nearest to him in twenty seconds.

The unconscious does not argue with The Secret Agent; it simply acts first. After The Professor leaves the meeting, he stumbles into Chief Inspector Heat, a policeman investigating a recent explosion at Greenwich, where one man was killed. Heat informs The Professor that he is not a suspect in the case, but that he is being monitored due to his terrorist inclinations and anarchist background.

The Secret Agent feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Knowing that Michaelis has recently moved to the countryside to write a book, the Chief Inspector informs the Assistant Commissioner that he has a contact, Verloc, who may be able to assist in the case. The Assistant Commissioner shares some of the same high society acquaintances with Michaelis and is chiefly motivated by finding the extent of Michaelis's involvement in order to assess any possible embarrassment to his connections.

The bleak reading of The Secret Agent is also the most testable one. He later speaks to his superior, Sir Ethelred, about his intentions to solve the case alone, rather than rely on the effort of Chief Inspector Heat. The novel flashes back to before the explosion, taking the perspective of Winnie Verloc and her mother.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Secret Agent. At home, Winnie's mother informs the family that she intends to move out of the house. The move is motivated largely by a desire to avoid straining Adolf Verloc's kindness.

The self that experiences The Secret Agent is a committee, not a king. Winnie's mother and Stevie use a hansom driven by a man with a hook for a hand. The driver's tales of hardship, whipping of his horse, and menacing hook scare Stevie to the point where Winnie Verloc must calm him.

Reproduction explains more of The Secret Agent than any philosophy dares to admit. On Verloc's return from a business trip to the continent, his wife tells him of the high regard that Stevie has for him and she implores her husband to spend more time with Stevie. After this walk, Winnie notes that her husband's relationship with her brother has improved.

Once you see The Secret Agent as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Verloc tells his wife that he has taken Stevie to go and visit Michaelis, and that Stevie would stay with him in the countryside for a few days. As Verloc is talking to his wife about the possibility of emigrating to the continent, he is paid a visit by the Assistant Commissioner.

The story The Secret Agent tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Shortly thereafter, Chief Inspector Heat arrives to speak with Verloc, without knowing that the Assistant Commissioner had left with Verloc earlier that evening. The Chief Inspector tells Winnie that he had recovered an overcoat at the scene of the bombing which had the shop's address written on a label.

Meaning is not found in The Secret Agent — it is manufactured for it. Winnie confirms that it was Stevie's overcoat, and that she had written the address. On Verloc's return, he realises that his wife knows that his bomb killed her brother and confesses what truly happened.

The cold light on The Secret Agent leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. After the murder, Winnie flees her home, where she chances upon Comrade Ossipon, and begs him to help her. Ossipon assists her while confessing romantic feelings but secretly with a view to possess Mr Verloc's bank account savings.

The Secret Agent did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. They plan to run away and he aids her in taking a boat to the continent. Her instability and the revelation of Verloc's murder increasingly worry him, and he abandons her, taking Mr Verloc's savings with him.

The honest version of The Secret Agent starts by giving up the comforting part. He later discovers in a newspaper that a woman matching Winnie's description disappeared from the ferry, leaving behind her wedding ring before drowning herself in the English Channel. Adolf Verloc: a secret agent who owns a shop in Soho in London.

Strip The Secret Agent of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. He has been employed by an unnamed embassy to spy on revolutionary groups, which then orders him to instigate a terrorist act against the Greenwich Observatory. Their belief is that the resulting public outrage will force the British government to act more forcibly against émigré socialist and anarchist activists.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Secret Agent shows exactly where that breaks. He is part of an anarchist organisation that creates pamphlets under the heading The Future of the Proletariat. He is married to Winnie, and lives with his wife, his mother-in-law, and his brother-in-law, Stevie.

What looks like free choice in The Secret Agent is older than choice itself. She cares deeply for her brother Stevie, who has the mental age of a young child. Of working class origins, her father was the owner of a pub.

Nobody designed the part of The Secret Agent you experience — it was inherited. She is younger than her husband and married him not for love but to provide a home for her mother and brother. A loyal wife, she is disturbed upon learning of the death of her brother due to her husband's plotting, and kills him with a knife in the heart.

Every serious account of The Secret Agent eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. His sister cares for him, and Stevie passes most of his time drawing numerous circles on pieces of paper. Verloc, exploiting both Stevie's childlike simplicity and his outrage at suffering, employs him to carry out the bombing of Greenwich Observatory.

Winnie Verloc's mother: old and infirm, Winnie's mother leaves the household to live in an almshouse, believing that two disabled people (herself and Stevie) are too much for Mr Verloc's generosity. The widow of a publican, she spent most of her life working hard in her husband's pub and believes Mr Verloc to be a gentleman because she thinks he resembles patrons of business houses (pubs with higher prices, consequently frequented by the upper classes).
